title: Stream-reconciliation and checkpointed capture protocol for robust multi-stream decode
creator: Diego Moreno
description:
Background: Our multi-stream decode path occasionally triggers expensive full recapture of the GPU capture graph when streams diverge during prefill/decode handoff. These recaptures increase p95 latency and create intermittent correctness concerns under preemption or heterogeneous batch shapes. Existing mitigations (full-stream quiesce and global barriers) are too heavyweight for high-concurrency service tiers and lead to throughput regressions.

Goal: Design and implement a lightweight stream-reconciliation protocol plus checkpointed capture points that: (1) limit full recaptures to pathological cases, (2) allow idempotent replay of segments, (3) retain kernel affinity information so the runtime selects the correct kernels after partial replay, and (4) keep memory and runtime overhead low enough for Dedicated and Hosted tiers. Acceptance targets: recapture rate < 0.5% on production-like traces, end-to-end p95 latency increase <= 5% vs baseline, correctness verified by deterministic replay tests.

Design proposal (high level):
- Epoched capture framing: each capture has a monotonic epoch id. Streams advertise their active epoch and a lightweight fence token (GPU event + epoch counter) on handoff.
- Checkpoint snapshots: at prefill boundary and at configurable decode windows we take compact checkpoints that include: KV-cache metadata (shape, offsets), logical sequence cursor, and a small checksum of attention masks. We avoid full tensor checkpointing unless triggered by mismatch.
- Reconciliation protocol: when a stream detects an epoch mismatch on replay, it attempts a local reconciliation using the last checkpoint and a bounded set of deterministic kernel replays. Only if reconciliation fails do we escalate to a full recapture.
- Kernel-affinity map: maintain a per-model, runtime-updated map keyed by (seq_len_bucket, batch_size, dtype, attention_mask_pattern) -> preferred kernel variant. When replaying, the runtime consults the map and binds kernels deterministically to avoid kernel-selection drift.
- Lazy/partial checkpointing: to control memory, checkpoints are compact and stored on-device in bump-allocated arenas with LRU eviction based on stream priority.
- Safety and idempotence: replayable fragments are marked and executed idempotently; side-effecting ops (profiling counters, ephemeral debug hooks) are suppressed during replay.

Implementation plan / milestones:
1) Spike: implement epoch header + event fence proof-of-concept integrated into capture/replay loop. Measure handshake latency and memory cost. (Done)
2) Checkpoint encoding: compact on-device snapshot format and LRU arena. Add basic eviction policy and metrics. (In progress)
3) Reconciliation flow: implement deterministic re-execution path for small fragment replays, tie into kernel-affinity map. Add feature flag to toggle reconciliation.
4) Tests and harness: randomized interleaving harness, preemption injection (simulate CUDA stream preemption), and deterministic golden-replay suite across sequence-length distributions.
5) Rollout: Canary on dedicated pool with low-traffic model, then staged ramp.

Risks & trade-offs:
- Memory vs recapture: checkpoints consume device memory (~40-150MB per GPU depending on model). We mitigate with compact encoding and eviction, but large-model tails must be careful.
- Complexity: additional code-paths increase maintenance burden; prefer opt-in feature flag and runtime metrics to safely roll back.
- Kernel drift: relying on kernel-affinity map requires good coverage or we risk subtle perf regressions; mitigation is A/B experiments and automatic fallback to safe kernels.

Metrics to track:
- recapture_rate (per-model, per-pool)
- reconciliation_success_rate
- p50/p95/p99 latency before/after for decode and total request
- memory_used_by_checkpoints (per-GPU)
- kernel_selection_changes_during_replay

Related artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/runtime/stream-recon-protocol
- Spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4876
- Checkpoint encoding draft: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1a2B3cStreamCheckpointDraft

Acceptance criteria:
- deterministic-harness shows 100% correctness across 1k randomized seeds
- recapture_rate <= 0.5% on production traces (sampled over 24h)
- no >5% regression in p95 latency in dedicated pool canary
- feature gated with telemetry and ability to disable per-pool
comments: 2026-02-18 Diego Moreno: Created ticket after spike showed epoch header handshake adds ~120us median and ~1.2MB overhead per active stream. Spoke with Aisha and Claire, agreed to pursue compact checkpoints rather than naive full-tensor copies.

2026-02-25 Aisha Patel: Implemented initial checkpoint arena. Observed 85MB/device for medium GPT-style model in naive layout. Switched to compressed offsets and reduced to ~28MB/device. Pushed spike PR (github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4876).

2026-03-02 Claire Zhang (review): Liked epoch fencing approach. Concern: eviction policy could bias high-priority customers. Suggested adding priority-weighted LRU; flagged security review for checkpoint metadata exposure (not full tensors).
2026-03-05 Samir Gupta (PM): Requested benchmarks on preemption scenarios and multi-tenant pools. Added task to run preemption injection on p3dn and on a local emulated preemptible instance.

2026-03-09 Aisha Patel: Added kernel-affinity map prototype. Deterministic binding reduced kernel-selection mismatches during replay from ~2.2% to 0.04% in synthetic runs. Preparing deterministic-harness tests.

2026-03-12 Diego Moreno: Integration test failed on heterogeneous batch shapes (dynamic batching edge-case). Added fallback path to perform compact recapture when shape sets broaden beyond reconciliation window. Pending test fixes.

2026-03-14 Aisha Patel: Marking feature flag ready for canary. Scheduling canary rollout 2026-03-20 to pool dedicated-low-traffic. Monitoring dashboards and alerts configured: recapture_rate and reconciliation_success_rate.
Follow-ups: refine eviction policy, add encryption for on-device checkpoint metadata, and add end-to-end regressions for function-calling workloads.
